intro: Before you, cut into the rock above a spring, is the İvriz Rock Relief, a monument in Konya province from the 8th century BC. This Neo-Hittite relief shows King Warpalawas standing before Tarhunzas, the storm god, with ears of grain and a bunch of grapes.
history: In the eighth century BC, Warpalawas, king of Tuwana, had himself and Tarhunzas, the god of plenty, carved into the rock above this spring. The result is among the largest works of Neo-Hittite art. Look closely: the god, shown nearly twice the king's height, holds a sheaf of grain and a bunch of grapes.
highlights: As you wander, don't miss the main rock relief, the Luwian hieroglyphic inscription, the spring and its pool, and the gorge of the Ambar stream.
facts: Did you know? The grain and grapes in the god's hands are among the earliest known images of a deity holding the produce of farming — a god's bounty made visible — and the same iconography reappears in the region's art centuries later. The god is shown nearly twice the king's height, because in Neo-Hittite art scale is the standard way of stating rank.
outro: This brings our tour of the İvriz Rock Relief to an end. Please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. Thank you for listening, and enjoy your visit.
